title: Compassion

lines: A FUNERAL AT THE GATE OF NAIN.
THE ONLY SON OF A WIDOW.
cards: A funeral is coming out through the gate of a town called Nain. A young man is being carried out on a bier. Luke gives the detail that makes it unbearable: he was "the only son of his mother, and she was a widow."
A crowd from the town walks with her. Coming up the road the other way is Jesus, with his own crowd. Two processions meet at the gate.
Nobody asks him for anything. Luke says that when he saw her, something moved in him before he said a word or lifted a hand.

teach.h: SUFFER WITH, NOT PITY FROM ABOVE.
teach.b: Some readers hear two Latin pieces inside the English word compassion: with, and suffering. Suffer with: not pity handed down, but feeling it from beside.
The Gospels' word goes lower still: "And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said unto her, Weep not."

The Greek verb is splanchnizomai, and some readers hear in it the gut: being moved in your insides. You met that gut-deep word back on day one hundred eighty-three, with a crowd like sheep without a shepherd.
Luke uses it of the Samaritan who stops for the man left half dead on the Jericho road: "he had compassion on him."
And of the father in the parable of the lost son: "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." Notice the order.
The feeling comes first, then the body moves. Jesus touches the bier, and the young man sits up. The Samaritan goes to him and binds up his wounds.
The father runs. Compassion here isn't a mood; it ends in the hands and feet.
Last, Paul makes it a job for ordinary people: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." And: "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ."
Some Christians link it to yesterday: if God suffers with people, following him means doing the same. It doesn't answer why there is suffering. It answers a different question: what now?

how: Christians practice compassion by visiting the sick and grieving, bringing meals, sitting with the dying and giving to those in need; churches organize care teams, hospital chaplaincies and works of mercy.

o: forgiving someone who has deeply wronged you
suffering with someone, then acting to help them
feeling sorry for someone from a safe distance

p: the father of the lost son

s: compassion means pity from a safe distance
it's suffering with: feeling it from beside, then staying close.
in Luke, the father runs to meet his lost son
"had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him."
at Nain, Jesus spoke to the widow only after raising her son
first he had compassion on her and said, "Weep not."

games.q: you're Jesus, meeting a funeral at the gate of Nain: a widow's only son. nobody has asked you for anything. what do you do?
o: step aside and let the procession pass.
have compassion, say "weep not," and touch the bier.
teach the crowd about death and heaven.
games.why: he had compassion on her, said "Weep not," and touched the bier, and the young man sat up. nobody had asked.

practice: Choose someone hurting whom you could actually reach, and picture the conversation: notice the pull to keep it short, to cheer them up, to fix it, and picture yourself staying instead, listening longer than is comfortable, letting a silence sit.

If you pray, you can bring them to God; if you don't, let the picture of staying be enough for now. And if they ever say they're in danger, in the US you can call or text 988 together, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Compassion. Suffering with someone: being moved inside, and then staying close.

orig.note: Greek: to be moved with compassion, a word some readers link with the inward parts. used of Jesus at Nain, the Samaritan, and the father of the lost son.

carryVoice: Your line: suffer with. Feeling first, then the hands. Go gently today, and I'll see you tomorrow.
